The reference implies that native_decide is bug-free correct and cannot be used to prove False. The reference implies that native_decide merely have increased trust base, i. e. requires trust in whole Lean compiler as opposed to just kernel, but otherwise native_decide is correct, i. e. cannot be used to prove False, unless there is a bug in that increased trust base (i. e. in whole Lean compiler).

I. e. the reference implies that the only way to prove False using native_decide is to find yet unknown Lean bug.

For example, the reference says:
===
Unlike {tactic}native_decide, {tactic}decide_cbv does not require trust in the code generator
===

BUT, as practice shows, this is not true. This is very easy to prove False using native_decide without exploiting any yet-unknown bugs in Lean. For example:

def a := 2

@[implemented_by a]
def b := 3

theorem x : b = 2 := by native_decide
theorem y : b = 3 := rfl
theorem z : False := by grind [x, y]

So, this means that either this code should be fixed, either the reference should be updated to explicitly say that not only by native_decide enlarges trust base (i. e. can be exploited by yet-unknown bugs only), but it is simply unsound and can be easily exploited by already-known Lean behavior. Ideally, this code snippet should be inserted to the reference

This is well known. Using implemented_by places the burden on the user to ensure that the claim is correct. There are also many other ways to prove False using native_decide (and even somewhat beyond native_decide depending on how the proof is checked, see comparator for the strictest way of checking).

I'm not sure if there's any docs page to link to that explains comprehensively what one should expect here...
(When you're quoting the reference, it would be helpful if you add links to the precise places)
OK. Thank you for answer. Then the reference should be fixed. Namely, docs for native_decide and chapter on axioms

===

or something similar

Does the reference for implemented_by not already cover this?

Instructs the compiler to use a different function as the implementation of a function. With the exception of tactics that call native code such as native_decide, the kernel and type checking are unaffected. When this attribute is used on a function, the function is not compiled and all compiler-related attributes (e.g. noncomputable, @[inline]) are ignored. Calls to this function are replaced by calls to its implementation.

The most common use cases of @[implemented_by] are to provide an efficient unsafe implementation and to make an unsafe function accessible in safe code through an opaque function:

unsafe def testEqImpl (as bs : Array Nat) : Bool :=
ptrEq as bs || as == bs

@[implemented_by testEqImpl]
def testEq (as bs : Array Nat) : Bool :=
as == bs

unsafe def printAddrImpl {α : Type u} (x : α) : IO Unit :=
IO.println s!"Address: {ptrAddrUnsafe x}"

@[implemented_by printAddrImpl]
opaque printAddr {α : Type u} (x : α) : IO Unit

The provided implementation is not checked to be equivalent to the original definition. This makes it possible to prove False with native_decide using incorrect implementations. For a safer variant of this attribute that however doesn't work for unsafe implementations, see @[csimp], which requires a proof that the two functions are equal.

Note that you can still prove false by tagging an unsafe declaration with csimp:

def f := 1
def g := 2

@[csimp]
unsafe def bad : f = g := lcProof

example : False := by
  have : f = g := by native_decide
  cases this
Maybe this was mentioned before: There is also #print opaques which is helpful for detecting things the kernel can't analyze but aren't axioms.
Improvements to that command are welcome in Batteries.

As well as I understand, #print opaques x prints definitions, introduced using keyword opaque, used inside of definition of x. But such opaque definitions are absolutely harmless (assuming they are not combined with actually dangerous features, such as implemented_by). opaque definitions are (in some sense) "absolutely irreducible definitions". That is. So, they are harmless.

On the other hand, implemented_by is dangerous. And yet (as well as I understand) there is no way to detect whether given definition involves something implemented using implemented_by.

So, we have very unfortunate situation: totally harmless opaque is detectable, but actually dangerous things (such as implemented_by) are not
As I said: "mprovements to that command are welcome"
Note that finalizing the compiler is not in the FRO timeline for 2026. So it's too early for many things that depend on specific compiler behavior.

See https://lean-lang.org/fro/roadmap/

If you are expecting a fully finalized Lean, you will have to wait for a few years. That doesn't mean it's not usable right now, but all Lean programs right now are "experimental" in a sense and will need to be updated regularly for the next few years until Lean stabilizes...

I'm totally okay with lack of compatibility. I just want Lean programming to have at least same strong guarantees that Lean proving has. And even if this not the case, then at least this should be documented

Kyle Miller said:

I think it makes sense for native_decide to mention implemented_by as increasing the trust base, so caveat emptor

Kyle's suggestion here would be included in the reference manual (since it contains the docstring for native_decide in the place you linked - do you think this would be sufficient to explain the confusion here?
Mostly yes. But it should say not "increasing the trust base", but "can prove False, for example, by using implemented_by or other methods". And, ideally, the same thing to chapter "Axioms"

I don't think it's a good idea to just say something unspecific like "beware that native_decide can be used to prove False in various ways, e.g. using implemented_by". That sounds like native_decide would be entirely unreliable. Instead I would say something like
Due to using the compiler, native_decide increases the trust base, specifically to:

  1. The compiler and interpreter itself
  2. All axioms the goal depends on
  3. @[implemented_by] and @[extern] attributes on functions the goal depends on
  4. All axioms used for the proofs of @[csimp] lemmas on functions the goal depends on
  5. unsafe terms used in functions the goal definitions on
  6. All custom compiler passes (i.e. @[cpass] attributes)
Wow, cool
Yes, let's do this

One observation I have here is Lean lacks of a single keyword that signals "allows inconsistency" (think Rust's unsafe), so one needs to keep extending this list in the doc when new features are added. I wonder if such keyword should be introduced
It might also be a good idea to make #print axioms or some other command look through all of these things and show them to the user
And I guess somewhere in there it should be mentioned that ST.Ref.get, ST.Ref.swap and ST.Ref.ptrEq cannot be trusted for native_decide (because ST is not opaque).

If you're curious, here's a proof of False using ST.Ref.get:

Proof of False

def test : ST ω Nat := fun s =>
  let ⟨ref, s₁⟩ := ST.Prim.mkRef 0 s
  let ⟨n, _⟩ := ST.Prim.Ref.get ref s₁
  let ⟨(), s₃⟩ := ST.Prim.Ref.set ref 1 s₁
  ⟨n, s₃⟩

def test2 : ST ω Nat := fun s =>
  let ⟨ref, s₁⟩ := ST.Prim.mkRef 0 s
  let ⟨(), s₃⟩ := ST.Prim.Ref.set ref 1 s₁
  let ⟨n, _⟩ := ST.Prim.Ref.get ref s₁
  ⟨n, s₃⟩

example : False := by
  have : (test (Void.mk ())).1 = 0 := by native_decide
  have : (test2 (Void.mk ())).1 = 1 := by native_decide
  have : @test = @test2 := rfl
  simp_all

I wonder if such keyword should be introduced

Yes, OTOH it could result in function coloring of anything that depends on any axioms (including sorry). I imagine there are a few Lean codebases with axioms (I believe #PrimeNumberTheorem+ (transitively) depends on native_decide), and that'll degrade their UX.
How about instead adding a set_option that'll make Lean show a warning next to decls that depend on any axioms? (like "this declaration uses sorry" but inherited)

In my ideal world (Lean 6, say),

  • when Alice runs #print axioms Bob.someTheorem she can distinguish (1) and (2) above from 3–6. (She trusts the leanprover codebase significantly more than Bob.)
  • Bob can use Carol's docs#Nat.fastFib_eq equivalent to implement a csimp and Carol's axioms appear when Alice makes that call
  • (the very hard part(?):) the #print axioms output is somehow ergonomic and human readable when using libraries with a lot of FFI or compiler optimisation

Should #print axioms ever become the tool to look at potentially adversarial code? Or is that something better left to tools like Comparator? (For non-adversarial code, it's obviously a great tool that can be improved further as you describe)
No because adversarial lean code can apparently change what #print axioms does
(It can, and it's not that hard.)

I'm trying to narrow down the misconception at work here and why it's evidently confusing. Two things are true:

  • native_decide introduces new axioms, and any bugs in the compiler could mean that reliance on these new axioms lead to bogus results
  • Many, many features of lean: @[implemented_by], metaprogramming features, and many more including those @Robin Arnez lists, allow you to modify the behavior of the lean compiler.

I'd suggest that the original example doesn't "reveal" a bug so much as it it adds a bug to the lean compiler — to the trusted code base that native_decide relies on to ensure it doesn't add bogus axioms — and then exercises it, causing native_decide to add a bogus axiom.

I don't think https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/#validating-proofs has been mentioned yet, which is a very good description of issues discussed here. This should probably be linked to from https://leanprover-community.github.io/did_you_prove_it.html
